title: Middle Powers at a Crossroads: Malaysia-Mexico Mobility-Centered Collaboration Amidst Rising U.S.-China Tensions
text:
Middle Powers at a Crossroads: Malaysia-Mexico Mobility-Centered Collaboration Amidst Rising U.S.-China Tensions

Photo by akinbostanci via Getty Images

Stepping off the plane in Kuala Lumpur, the air coming in through the cracks of the corridor is thick from the heat. Quickly, the kindness of Malaysian people becomes apparent. On the drive to my hotel, I had a long conversation about family with the cab driver. Hearing the way he described his childhood felt familiar; it felt like home. While Mexico and Malaysia are far geographically, both have rich cultures and people who have an unwavering determination to succeed, the contagious type that cannot be taught.Unfortunately, determination today is simply not enough. The world is highly complex and geopolitically unstable. Global value chains are in flux, economies are still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, and the effects of the ongoing U.S.-China economic rivalry continues. Every country is having to go back to the drawing board to rework their strategies to stay afloat during this storm.In this context, Malaysia finds itself at a critical crossroad, working towards becoming a regional innovation hub while simultaneously navigating geopolitical tensions and trade wars. Walking around the Malaysian Research Accelerator for Technology & Innovation (MRANTI), it is evident that the country is on the right path. For example, MRANTI goes beyond the typical research and development (R&D) and works on harnessing technology, such as using 5G and AI technology to reduce agricultural losses. By leveraging climate data, it can optimize soil conditions and agricultural outputs. However, investment and industrial policy alone are not the answer.There is an unexplored opportunity for Malaysia to strengthen partnerships with other middle powers to achieve its goal of becoming a regional innovation hub. While countries are turning to protectionist policies and closing their borders, that “risk” can be turned on its head and become an opportunity for countries willing to go against the grain. Malaysia can be innovative in rethinking how it approaches mobility: the circulation of innovation, technology, and talent.While Malaysia could opt to try this mobility-centered collaboration with another ASEAN country, there are limitations. First, intra-ASEAN trade has been stagnating. Second, there is a mismatch in development across the region—disparities in the maturity of their tech industries and advanced manufacturing may restrict Malaysia from solely focusing on intra-ASEAN trade. Finally, the fragmentation within ASEAN is exacerbated amidst the unstable geopolitical landscape, South China Sea tensions, and tariffs against the bloc. ASEAN countries are increasingly seeking out individual strategies to reduce their vulnerabilities, therefore, making it more difficult for Malaysia to develop a mobility-centered collaboration within the region.The answer may lie across the Pacific. Upon first glance, Mexico may not seem like the obvious choice. The two countries are typically presented as competitors for foreign direct investment (FDI) and alternatives to China (‘China +1’) for American and European companies looking to reduce supply chain overdependency by expanding their operations into other markets. Not to mention, the trade landscape is a sore point—Malaysians are not thrilled about Mexico’s tariffs and actions towards decreasing imports from Asia.However, a closer examination paints a different picture.Malaysia and Mexico are both members of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC). Mexico also offers a skilled talent pool, plus complementary industrial and scientific capabilities. A renewed Malaysia-Mexico relationship for the 21st century that focuses on scientific exchanges, technology sharing, and a bilateral talent corridor will unlock the missing puzzle piece Malaysia needs to become a regional innovation hub.Three pillars of a strengthened Malaysia-Mexico partnershipScientific ExchangesBecoming an AI nation will be achieved faster by fostering scientific exchanges. Malaysia and Mexico can leverage their respective universities to conduct research on shared interest areas (e.g. semiconductors, AgTech, AI, and renewable energy). They can also develop joint degree programs for Malaysian students to study robotics and renewable energy in Mexico, while Mexican students study AI and smart manufacturing in Malaysia. In addition to this, they can pursue government-subsidized grants that explore innovations for uplifting populations out of poverty—such initiatives would be aligned with Malaysia’s MADANI framework. A promising example is Amaziasizamoria Jumail’s work through the Merdeka Award Grant for International Attachment exploring tropical forest restoration in Mexico and bringing insights back to the Regrow Borneo project in Malaysia.Technology SharingMalaysia has a mature semiconductor ecosystem due to its 50 years of experience and enabling infrastructure. Mexico has strong automotive and robotics industries. Mexico also offers a lot of advantages, from trade openness, close proximity to U.S. markets, and an innovative environment. Bilateral technology-sharing on industries they excel in, with mutual safeguards to protect national security concerns, is critical for Malaysia and Mexico to remain competitive. Both countries also share concerns over climate change’s impact on food security. They can explore innovative AgTech, which includes all products, tools, solutions, and software across the entire agriculture value chain. By collaborating, the two countries can modernize their agricultural capabilities and diminish vulnerabilities of small-scale farmers whose livelihoods depend on their harvests. Finally, through CPTPP, they can improve access to markets for their small and medium enterprises (SMEs) working in agriculture.Bilateral Talent CorridorMalaysia is struggling with finding talent. Creating a new migration scheme would allow for easier circulation of talent between middle-income countries. With Mexico, Malaysia can implement the first of its kind reciprocal circular migration initiative for high skilled labor—e.g. engineers, scientists, and AI researchers. The CPTPP already allows temporary movement, but this would be an expansion for longer periods. Cooperation on a bilateral talent corridor can reduce bureaucracy for work visas to create easier access to their respective job markets and implement tax and relocation incentives to ensure that talent is attracted and retained. This would help ease labor shortages.Mexico is the missing puzzle pieceMalaysia’s innovation depends on reimagining its mobility. Its ambitions will remain unfulfilled if it does not get the science, technology, and talent it needs. Mexico offers the perfect sounding board to test a new model of middle-power partnership for the 21st century. Competition should not stand in the way of collaboration. Enhancing Malaysia-Mexico relations can be the springboard towards more partnerships between middle power countries caught in between major powers.

About the Author

Itziri Gonzalez Barcenas is a former DACA recipient born in Mexico and raised in the United States, shaped by a life lived across borders. She studied at Davidson College, Sciences Po Paris, and Tsinghua University. Her work has taken her to UN agencies, the OECD, academic institutions, and nonprofits around the world.
